conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in last night for chest pain after using cocaine, alcohol, and heroin. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m okay now. The chest pain was sharp but only lasted a few seconds. I’ve had it before, about once a month. But I got scared because I also passed out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your brother said you lost consciousness for a few seconds but came back quickly, no confusion or weakness after. That’s important. We’ve reviewed your EKG and blood tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it another heart attack? It felt like my old ones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your troponin levels—those tell us if there’s heart muscle damage—were normal both times we checked. That’s reassuring. Your EKG shows old changes from prior heart damage, but no new heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why the chest pain and passing out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history of heart disease and the cocaine use, we think this was demand ischemia—your heart needed more oxygen than it could get, especially with cocaine narrowing your blood vessels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the passing out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could be related to the same thing—sudden drop in blood flow or rhythm change from the cocaine. But your heart rhythm was stable here, and neuro exam is normal. No signs of seizure or stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to go. My nephew’s wake is today. I need to be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But before you go, we need to make sure you’re safe. We’ve had psychiatry evaluate you—they agree you’re not a danger to yourself or others.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not suicidal. I just use to cope. But I know it’s bad for my heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And that’s why we’re stressing this: cocaine is extremely dangerous with your heart condition. It can trigger a fatal heart attack. We strongly recommend stopping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my meds? I take metoprolol, aspirin, Plavix, the usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep taking aspirin, Plavix, and your statin. But—and this is critical—do not take metoprolol if you use cocaine. The combination can cause severe low blood pressure or heart rhythm issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know that. I’ll stop the cocaine. I promise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also sent info on addiction counseling with social work. Please follow up with your PCP and counselor. Your heart function is reduced—about 36%—so staying healthy is crucial.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Can I go now? I don’t have the chest pain anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re medically stable to go home. But please, take the discharge instructions seriously. Avoid all substances, especially cocaine, and follow up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doc. I’ll try to do better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you a nicotine patch to help with smoking, and your other meds are listed. If you have chest pain again, go to the ER immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your urine test showed cocaine, opiates, and benzos. Mixing those with your heart condition is very risky. Please talk to your counselor about this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I’ll bring it up. Thanks for not keeping me longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re stable now, but your choices going forward matter a lot. Take care of yourself. Your PCP needs to know about the clonazepam and alcohol too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call them. I just need to get to the wake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright. You’re discharged. Go home safely, and please follow up within a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.
